children: The global financial system is under an intensifying threat from cyberattacks, with software providers barely keeping pace with advances in hacking technology, the International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday.

In more than 70% of reported attacks so far this year, software providers had almost no time to patch vulnerabilities before attackers exploited them, the IMF said in its latest update on financial stability.
That's more than double the share in 2021, when providers typically had close to 300 days to fix vulnerabilities, it added.

Frontier artificial-intelligence models could accelerate both attacks and defenses, increasing the importance of cyber resilience, incident reporting, crisis preparedness, and oversight of critical third-party providers, the IMF said.
"Cyberattacks are a growing risk, especially those targeting payments, trading, access to deposits, or other critical financial services," it added.

The comments come amid broadening international calls to slow the advance of AI and regulate the industry to better control the technology, something that President Trump has rejected, advocating instead for a soft-touch approach.
The IMF also warned that the boom in investment in artificial intelligence could badly rock financial markets if it starts to stumble.

To be sure, investment in data centers, semiconductors and related infrastructure has spurred economic activity, while companies driving the AI boom have delivered exceptional earnings growth, it said.
But "faltering AI investment and profitability could challenge optimistic expectations and trigger a correction in asset prices linked to the AI industry," the report said.

Growing leverage could be a catalyst for such a correction, the IMF added. "Hyperscalers, as the largest data-center operators are known, are borrowing more and more, while investors have been leveraging to invest in AI stocks."

Circular financing arrangements in the AI sector, involving equity and debt flows between AI firms, suggest that stress at key companies receiving investment could quickly lower revenue forecasts, it said.

The IMF's review of 14 such transactions since 2023 found that about $300 billion dollars in equity investments and $650 billion dollars in debt are leveraged against $1.4 trillion in future revenue commitments.
Sovereign bond yields have also risen sharply amid renewed inflation pressures from higher energy prices, fiscal concerns, and, in some cases, stronger-than-expected economic growth, it said.
"It may be the case that bond yields are moving back toward the levels seen before the global financial crisis, when growth and inflation were higher than in the 2010s," the IMF added.
As government bonds underpin the global financial system, the consequences of higher sovereign yields could extend well beyond public debt, it warned.
For now, financial markets remain resilient amid solid economic growth and strong corporate earnings, while financial conditions have been relatively accommodative," the IMF said.
"However, there is no room for complacency," it added. "Vulnerabilities beneath the surface could determine how damaging the manifestation of these risks would be."
